title: The Fake Dosa Makers: How AI-Generated Videos Are Weaponising Indian Street Food
excerpt: Millions of views, zero reality — AI-generated clips depicting unsanitary Indian food preparation are going viral, and the diaspora is paying the reputational price.
body:
They look real enough to make you gag. A shirtless man kneading dough on his bare stomach. Another frying bread with his feet. A vendor pouring what appears to be gutter water into a biryani pot. These viral videos — racking up tens of millions of views on TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts — claim to show the grotesque underbelly of Indian street food. There is just one problem: they are entirely fabricated by artificial intelligence.

A recent investigation by Lead Stories, an accredited fact-checking organisation, found that a growing number of these viral clips are generated using AI video tools, most notably OpenAI's Sora. The videos share a common formula — a busy Indian street market setting, a man preparing food in deliberately shocking ways, over-the-top camera angles, and captions like "Only in India" or "Would you eat this?" They are, in the language of the internet, AI slop — but the kind of slop that carries a sharply racist payload.

## The Anatomy of a Fake

The tell-tale signs are there if you know where to look. Hands blur and merge unnaturally. Rolling pins morph into the dough they are supposed to flatten. Background figures stand perfectly still while the foreground action unfolds. In one widely shared clip, a man appears to dip bread into oil with his bare feet, but a frame-by-frame analysis reveals impossible physics — the bread changes shape mid-air, and the vendor's toes phase through the pan.

Fact-checking organisations across the globe have flagged dozens of these clips. India's DFRAC identified the TikTok account @indianstreetfoodonly, which posts exclusively AI-generated content depicting Indian vendors in unsanitary conditions. With over 35,000 followers, its most-viewed video crossed 40 million plays. Other accounts, including @fakerealmoments and @rovert.red, follow the same playbook.

Hive Moderation, an AI-detection tool used by newsrooms and fact-checkers, has consistently rated these clips at 98 to 99 percent probability of being AI-generated. Yet the comments sections tell a different story — one where the audience has largely accepted the footage as real. "Delete India," reads one comment. "Imagine the smell," reads another.

## Why India, and Why Now?

The targeting is not random. Indian street food — with its open-air preparation, vibrant chaos, and unfamiliar textures — has long been a subject of fascination and, for some, discomfort on social media. AI video generators have simply weaponised that gap between curiosity and revulsion.

"When an account posts an AI video of an Indian street vendor on hygiene standards, people usually can identify that it is not real because an AI watermark is visible," DFRAC noted in its analysis. "But when the same video is carried forward to other platforms like X and Instagram, many suppose it to be real. The traction that these videos receive is immense, which only brings hate, humiliation, shame and a negative stereotype for Indians."

The phenomenon is not limited to food. Australia's AAP FactCheck has documented a parallel wave of AI-generated videos depicting Muslim women complaining about Australian food culture — the same production style, the same engagement-bait formula, the same dehumanising intent.

## The Diaspora's Double Bind

For Indian Americans and NRIs, these videos strike a particularly tender nerve. Many grew up defending their lunchboxes from mockery and their mothers' cooking from ridicule. The arrival of Indian cuisine at the summit of American fine dining — Michelin stars, James Beard awards, Whole Foods shelf space — was supposed to signal that the battle was won. Instead, AI has opened a new front.

The irony is that real Indian street food is thriving in America. Chai Pani just earned another James Beard nomination. Dahi Bhalla chaat is on the menu at a Michelin-starred restaurant in Hudson Yards. The world's best restaurants are studying Indian spice work with the seriousness once reserved for French mother sauces. But none of that goes viral the way a fake video of a man frying dosa batter with his toes does.

## What Can Be Done?

TikTok's community guidelines technically prohibit "misleading content created or altered by AI," but enforcement remains inconsistent. Many of the offending accounts include "AI" in their bios — a fig leaf of disclosure that platforms accept as sufficient, even when the content is reshared without context on other platforms.

Food activists and diaspora organisations are pushing for stronger platform enforcement, clearer AI watermarking standards, and, above all, media literacy. The next time a video of an Indian street vendor doing something impossible goes viral, the first question should not be "Is this real?" It should be "Who made this, and why?"

In the meantime, the best defence may be the simplest one: share the real thing. The sizzle of a tawa. The crack of a pani puri shell. The theatre of a chai wallah pouring from a height. Indian street food does not need AI to be extraordinary. It never did.

nri_angle: AI-generated fake videos depicting unsanitary Indian food preparation are fuelling anti-Indian stereotypes online, undercutting the diaspora's decades-long effort to gain respect for Indian cuisine in the West.
